rounds.verdict: Do not publish as-is: a sound pull-back idea, but the duck/toilet misregistration and clipped opening frame undermine it.
filmIssues: The pull-back reveal is legible — framing widens from the screen toward the full cinema and audience — but the duck does not stay registered on the toilet that belongs with it. Because the toilet is in the background and the duck is a depth-0.6 layer, the high opening zoom and pan slide the duck to the left rim of the bowl in the t=0 to t=0.4 frames, only settling into its painted, centred position by t=1. The opening picture therefore reads as misaligned rather than as a tight hero shot.
The 'settle' entrance compounds that separation, making the duck appear to drift across the seat instead of sitting solidly on it.

At the opening zoom the audience silhouettes are awkwardly clipped at the left, right and bottom frame edges, so t=0 is a cropped, off-register picture rather than a good page-opening image. The final full-frame picture is good to dwell on.
The light-sweep is fitting for a projector beam and is not distracting in the stills, and the cut-paper print style is preserved with no tearing or ghost duck visible.

rounds.verdict: A clear premiere reveal: starting on the film-within-the-film and pulling back to the laughing audience gives the motion a story purpose beyond a plain push-in, with a clean final hold.
filmIssues: The pull-back is clear and purposeful: it opens tight on the duck on the toilet inside the screen, then steadily widens and pans down to reveal the projector beam, full screen and audience rows, ending on the complete premiere picture.

The duck stays coherent and locked to the toilet seat throughout, with no tearing, doubled edges, halo or ghost from its painted-over spot. Its low depth and lack of drift keep cut-outs that belong together together.
The first frame is a strong close opening on the screen/duck and the last frame is the best dwell image — the full cinema composition with screen, beam and audience visible and in frame.
The light-sweep ambient is fitting for a projector/cinema scene and remains subtle in the stills; the cut-paper print style is preserved.
